question: to the Commission Per Clausen (The Left) Subject:

The latest extraterritorial sanctions from the US targeting Cuba have already led to many European companies, large and small, having to quickly abandon business in Cuba, in what the press has described as their fleeing the island1. This clearly means that US sanctions are already resulting in both direct and indirect costs for numerous European companies. Fortunately the EU has an instrument – the Blocking Statute23 – which can be used (and indeed has been used in the past) for exactly this type of situation. It is important that this, and other tools, be employed to counter US actions. In this regard: 1.

What specific actions is the European Commission planning to take to counter or mitigate the impact on European companies, following the latest US sanctions against Cuba and their extraterritorial nature?

Does the Commission have an estimate of the potential monthly losses, both direct and indirect, that European businesses – and by extension the European economy – might incur as a result of these sanctions, and if not, when will one be produced?
When will the EU’s Blocking Statute be triggered in response to this situation, as it was with the 1996 US sanctions?

answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.8.2026) The Commission has consistently maintained that the extra-territorial application of secondary sanctions is incompatible with international law and that sanctions must comply with the UN Charter, international humanitarian law and due process. The assessment of third-country extraterritorial sanctions on Cuba should be framed also within the EU’s commitment to safeguard legitimate trade and investment. Where the new executive orders can be considered as an action based on or resulting from an act specified in the Annex of Regulation 2271/96 (Blocking Statute)1, including the Helms Burton Act, then the latter regulation already protects the EU operators by prohibiting compliance with that executive order. Information obtained under the Blocking Statute Regulation pertains to the effects of the laws, regulations and other legislative instruments included in its Annex. The Commission does not have access to company-level data that would allow an estimate of foregone income to be made; such an estimate is further complicated by the difficulty in assessing the counterfactual (if companies were to continue operations in Cuba but under conditions of fuel and other restrictions). The fundamental concern for the EU is that there be a level playing field for all foreign investors in Cuba.
